references.text: In the parable of the friend who comes at midnight, Jesus teaches that persistent prayer leads to an answer. This parable shares the same theme as the parable of the unjust judge – both encourage perseverance in prayer ([ref:Luk 11:5-10|Luke 11:5-10]).
Jesus urges his disciples to stay awake and pray at all times, reflecting the call in Luke 18:1 to always pray and not lose heart ([ref:Luk 21:36|Luke 21:36]).

Paul urges believers to continue steadfastly in prayer and to be watchful with thanksgiving – a direct parallel to Jesus' teaching on always praying and not losing heart ([ref:Kol 4:2|Colossians 4:2]).
Paul's exhortation "Pray without ceasing" summarizes the core message of Luke 18:1 that we should always pray ([ref:1 Tess 5:17|1 Thessalonians 5:17]).
Paul encourages praying at all times in the Spirit, with every kind of prayer and petition, and to persevere in this – reflecting Jesus' teaching on persistent prayer ([ref:Ef 6:18|Ephesians 6:18]).
Paul urges believers to be steadfast in prayer, which aligns with Jesus' message to always pray and not give up ([ref:Rom 12:12|Romans 12:12]).
Paul writes about not losing heart (ἐγκακεῖν) in service – the same Greek word used in Luke 18:1 regarding not giving up in prayer ([ref:2 Kor 4:1|2 Corinthians 4:1]).
Again, Paul uses the same word ἐγκακεῖν (to lose heart) and urges us not to give up, thematically reflecting Jesus' call at the beginning of the parable ([ref:2 Kor 4:16|2 Corinthians 4:16]).
Paul encourages us not to grow weary in doing good, with the promise that we will reap in due time if we do not give up – a related theme to not losing heart in prayer ([ref:Gal 6:9|Galatians 6:9]).

Jacob wrestled with God all night and refused to let go until he received a blessing – a classic example from the Old Testament of persistent prayer and not giving up ([ref:1 Mos 32:24-28|Genesis 32:24-28]).
